These individuals depend on various forms of assistive technology to maintain their independence, quality of life, and access to essential services. Key populations whose mobility might be impacted by a power outage include older adults, individuals with neurological conditions and musculoskeletal disorders, amputees, and those with spinal cord injuries. In addition, those with severe obesity or respiratory disorders may depend on mobility devices. Chronic conditions may indicate a higher understanding and planning for mobility needs during a power outage (e.g., manual wheelchair available, evacuation plan from building if elevator is out); however, temporary mobility challenges due to injury or recovery from surgery may result in lower levels of planning and resilience. Potential Distributed Actions: Individuals who are reliant on mobility equipment should have an emergency power plan or backup manual device to use in case of emergencies. Plans should include power alternatives (generator, batteries, or relocation if needed), clear instructions for how to obtain and connect devices, mobility device instruction manuals, and serial and model numbers. When creating an emergency power plan, individuals and their care teams should consider if equipment will need to be reset when power is reconnected (either temporarily or when power is restored). Potential Shared Solutions: Individuals needing to charge mobility devices should have priority access to charging at a resilience hub in order to ensure the health and safety of those individuals. Additionally, institutions or organizations with surplus supplies could check out their manual devices to individuals in need during power outages. Rationale: Ensuring the safety of individuals dependent on mobility devices during an emergency or power outage requires careful planning and proactive measures. First, individuals using wheelchairs should have a personalized emergency plan that includes accessible 37 evacuation routes, alternative exits, and assistance contacts. Keeping an emergency supply kit with essential medications, backup batteries, and a manual wheelchair as a contingency is crucial. Additionally, notifying building management or local emergency services about mobility needs in advance can help responders provide timely and appropriate assistance. For those who rely on elevators to exit a building, alternative escape strategies must be established in case of power failure. Identifying stairwell evacuation chairs, training designated personnel on their use, and practicing emergency drills can ensure a smooth evacuation. In multi-story buildings, individuals should work with management to determine designated areas of refuge where they can wait safely for assistance. Battery-powered stair lifts or portable ramps may also be considered for buildings with limited accessibility options. Finally, communication is key in any emergency. Individuals should maintain a charged mobile phone, an emergency contact list, and a whistle or flashlight to signal for help if necessary. Caregivers and building staff should be trained to assist those with mobility impairments, and emergency plans should be regularly reviewed and updated. By prioritizing preparedness, ensuring accessible evacuation routes, and fostering a supportive network, the safety of individuals dependent on mobility devices can be significantly enhanced during unexpected emergencies.
